paragraphs: We must note here that Fyodor Pavlovitch knew where to look for the weak spot. There had been malicious rumors at one time, which had even reached the Archbishop (and not only about our monastery, but about others where the institution of elders existed), that too much respect was paid to the elders, even to the detriment of the Superior’s authority, and that the elders abused the sacrament of confession, and so on and so on. These were absurd charges, which had died away of themselves everywhere. But the spirit of folly had caught hold of Fyodor Pavlovitch and was carrying him on the current of his own nerves into lower and lower depths of disgrace, and it prompted him with this old slander. Fyodor Pavlovitch did not understand a word of it, and he could not even put it sensibly, for on this occasion no one had been kneeling and confessing aloud in the elder’s cell, so he could not have seen anything of the kind. He was only speaking from a confused memory of old slanders. But as soon as he had uttered his foolish tirade, he felt he had been talking absurd nonsense. At once he longed to prove to his audience, and above all to himself, that he had not been talking nonsense. And though he knew perfectly well that with each word he would be adding more and more absurdity, he could not restrain himself and plunged blindly forward.
“How disgraceful!” cried Pyotr Alexandrovitch.

“Forgive me!” said the Father Superior. “It was said of old, ‘Many have begun to speak against me and have uttered evil sayings about me. And hearing it I have said to myself: it is the correction of the Lord and He has sent it to heal my vain soul.’ And so we humbly thank you, honored guest!” And he made Fyodor Pavlovitch a low bow.

“Tut—tut—tut—sanctimoniousness and stock phrases! Old phrases and old gestures. The old lies and formal bowing and scraping. We know all about them. A kiss on the lips and a dagger in the heart, as in Schiller’s _Robbers_. I don’t like falsehood, Fathers, I want the truth. But the truth isn’t to be found in eating gudgeon, and I proclaim that aloud! Father monks, why do you fast? Why do you expect a reward in heaven for that? Why, for a reward like that I’ll come and fast too! No, saintly monk, you try being virtuous in the world, do good to society, without shutting yourself up in a monastery at other people’s expense and without expecting a reward up above for it—you’ll find that a bit harder. I can talk sense too, Father Superior. What have they got here?” He went up to the table. “Old port wine, mead brewed by the Eliseyev Brothers. Fie, fie, Fathers! That’s a good step beyond gudgeon. Look at the bottles the fathers have brought out, he he he! And who provided it all? The Russian peasant, the laborer, brings here the farthing earned by his horny hand, wringing it from his family and the tax-gatherer! You bleed the people, you know, holy fathers.”
“This is too disgraceful!” said Father Iosif.
Father Païssy kept stubbornly silent. Miüsov rushed from the room, and Kalganov went after him.

“Well, Father, I’ll follow Pyotr Alexandrovitch! I’m not coming to see you again. You can beg me on your knees, I won’t come. I sent you a thousand roubles, so you’ve started keeping an eye on me. He he he! No, I’ll say no more. I’m taking my revenge for my youth, for all the humiliation I endured.” He thumped the table with his fist in a fit of pretended feeling. “This monastery has played a great part in my life! It has cost me many bitter tears. You used to turn my wife, the crazy one, against me. You cursed me with bell and book, you spread stories about me all over the place. Enough, fathers! This is the age of Liberalism, the age of steamers and railways. Neither a thousand roubles, nor a hundred, no, nor a hundred farthings will you get out of me!”

It must be noted again that our monastery had never played any great part in his life, and that he had never shed a bitter tear because of it. But he was so carried away by his pretended emotion that for one moment he almost believed it himself. He was so touched he almost wept. But at that very instant he felt it was time to draw back.
The Father Superior bowed his head at this malicious lie and again spoke impressively:
“It is written again, ‘Bear with care and gladness the dishonor that comes upon you through no act of your own. Do not be confounded, and do not hate the one who has dishonored you.’ And so will we.”

“Tut, tut, tut! Thinking it over, and the rest of the rigmarole. Think it over, Fathers, I’m off. But I’ll take my son Alexey away from here for ever, on my parental authority. Ivan Fyodorovitch, my most dutiful son, allow me to order you to follow me. Von Sohn, what have you to stay for? Come and see me now in town. It’s fun there. It’s only one short verst. Instead of lenten oil, I’ll give you sucking-pig and kasha. We’ll have dinner with some brandy and liqueur to go with it.... I’ve got cloudberry wine. Hey, von Sohn, don’t lose your chance.” He went out, shouting and gesticulating.
It was at that moment that Rakitin saw him and pointed him out to Alyosha.
“Alexey!” his father shouted from far off, catching sight of him. “You come home to me today, for good, and bring your pillow and mattress, and leave no trace behind.”

Alyosha stood rooted to the spot, watching the scene in silence. Meanwhile Fyodor Pavlovitch had got into the carriage, and Ivan was about to follow him in grim silence, without even turning to say goodbye to Alyosha. But at this point another almost incredible scene of grotesque buffoonery put the finishing touch on the episode. Maximov suddenly appeared beside the carriage. He ran up, panting, afraid of being too late. Rakitin and Alyosha saw him running. He was in such a hurry that in his impatience he put his foot on the step where Ivan’s left foot was still resting, and clutching the carriage, he kept trying to jump in. “I’m going with you!” he kept shouting, laughing a thin, merry laugh, with a look of reckless glee on his face. “Take me too.”

“There!” cried Fyodor Pavlovitch, delighted. “Didn’t I say he was von Sohn? It is von Sohn himself, risen from the dead. Why, how did you tear yourself away? What did you _vonsohn_ there? And how could you get away from the dinner? You must have a brazen face! I have one myself, but I’m surprised at you, brother! Jump in, jump in! Let him pass, Ivan. It’ll be fun. He can lie somewhere at our feet. Will you lie at our feet, von Sohn? Or perch on the box with the coachman. Skip up on the box, von Sohn!”
But Ivan, who had by now taken his seat, gave Maximov a violent punch in the chest without a word and sent him flying. It was only by chance that he did not fall.
“Drive on!” Ivan shouted angrily to the coachman.
“Why, what are you doing? What are you about? Why did you do that?” Fyodor Pavlovitch protested.
But the carriage had already driven off. Ivan made no reply.
“Well, you’re quite a fellow,” Fyodor Pavlovitch said again.
After a pause of two minutes, looking sideways at his son, he said, “Why, it was you who got up all this monastery business. You urged it, you approved of it. Why are you angry now?”
“You’ve talked enough rot. You might give it a rest now,” Ivan snapped sullenly.
Fyodor Pavlovitch was silent again for two minutes.
“A drop of brandy would be nice now,” he observed, as if uttering a great truth, but Ivan made no response.
“You’ll have some too, when we get home.”
Ivan was still silent.
Fyodor Pavlovitch waited another two minutes.
“But I’m going to take Alyosha away from the monastery, however much you dislike it, most honored Karl von Moor.”
Ivan shrugged his shoulders contemptuously and, turning away, stared at the road. And they did not speak again all the way home.
